articles.title: Houthis, Yemeni forces engaged in fierce battles: Why each front matters
articles.summary: Forces loyal to the UN-recognised government and Houthis fight on multiple fronts in an effort to expand their control.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – The United Nations-recognised Yemeni government and the Houthi group have been using warplanes, missiles, drones and other weapons as they engage in intense fighting on multiple fronts in the country’s north, west and central regions.

At least 194 people have been killed and 880 others wounded in the past two weeks of fighting in parts of Taiz, the western coast, al-Jawf, Marib and Dhalea, according to aid agencies.

Iran-backed Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), on Thursday reportedly seized Mocha, located on the western coast, gaining a foothold in the Red Sea – a vital shipping lane.

Government forces have been battling to expand in Taiz and boost their control of Marib, an oil-producing region in the north.

Fighting has also been raging in the al-Jawf governorate bordering Saudi Arabia and Dhalea, which connects the Houthi-controlled north to the country’s south under the internationally recognised government.

Experts say gains or losses on any of these strategically important fronts could have significant consequences for either side.

“The hills and mountainous areas of Taiz and the western coast are key targets for the Houthis, who have repeatedly attempted to advance there,” Yazeed al-Jeddawy, the research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, said.

“The Houthis are trying to seize commanding terrain, cut supply routes between the coastal Mocha district and Taiz, and prevent government troops on the western coast from linking up with the Taiz Military Axis,” said al-Jeddawy.

In Taiz and along the western coast, al-Jeddawy says, the immediate contest is over the heights and roads connecting Taiz to Mocha.

Situated roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Bab al-Mandeb strait, Mocha enjoys a highly strategic position on the Red Sea. The Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on the city last month, causing massive damage to its port facilities and killing and injuring several civilians. The group also extended its ground operations towards Mocha city.

“The Houthis seem intent on tightening their hold around Mocha and moving closer to the Dhubab–Bab al-Mandeb area. A substantial advance would strengthen their position near the southern entrance to the Red Sea and give them greater leverage over international shipping,” he said, before the Houthis reportedly seized Mocha.

Fuad Mussed, a Yemeni political analyst and author, told Al Jazeera that the strategic importance of the western coast and Taiz fronts stems from their proximity to Bab al-Mandeb, a chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

“The Houthis seek to move closer to this vital waterway to threaten maritime traffic. Such a move aims to keep the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb under the influence of Iran and use them as leverage against regional and international powers. This is a strategy Tehran has been pursuing for years,” Mussed said.

Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, to use it as leverage in the war against the United States. It has also warned that its allies could shut shipping via Bab al-Mandeb. Iran also attacked Saudi Arabia’s pipeline used to export oil from the Red Sea.

In July, the Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi vessels transiting through the Red Sea – an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the past few weeks, pro-government forces have attacked Houthi-held territories in Marib and al-Jawf, facing further retaliation from the Houthis.

Saddam al-Huraibi, a Yemeni political commentator, said the Marib front is fateful for both sides.

“Marib is a government stronghold in north Yemen. So, a Houthi expansion in Marib would threaten government presence and weaken its leverage in the north. That is why pro-government troops are ready to fight tooth and nail on this front line,” al-Huraibi told Al Jazeera.

For the Houthis, the takeover of Marib will deepen the group’s authority and step towards controlling the oil and gas infrastructure. The Iran-backed group captured vast swaths of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, but Marib has remained in government hands since.

“Dominating Marib’s oil and gas resources has been a Houthi goal for over a decade. Without facing a crushing defeat in Marib, they would keep fighting to achieve that goal,” al-Huraibi said.

Adjacent to Marib, al-Jawf is also a hub of tense fighting between the Houthis and government forces. A government gain there would lay the groundwork for further advances, while a strong Houthi defence could undermine government forces’ morale and prompt them to retreat.

“Government-aligned forces have lately focused much of their offensive effort on al-Jawf. Government gains in al-Jawf would ease the threat to Marib while requiring the Houthis to defend a much broader area,” al-Huraibi said.

Al-Jeddawy said government gains could open routes towards the north – Saada, Amran or Houthi positions north of Marib.

The Houthis have carried out attacks in Saudi Arabia, including energy facilities in the country’s south. They have also accused Saudi Arabia of launching multiple attacks in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz provinces in support of government forces.

Fighting on the Dhalea front, a strategic gateway between Houthi-held territory and the southern governorates, has intensified in recent weeks.

Fighting there did not fully stop during the relative calm, which began in April 2022 following the UN-brokered ceasefire.

A Houthi advance there could open a route for their fighters to reach other southern territories. On the other hand, a Houthi setback would encourage government forces to push towards Ibb, controlled by the group.

“[Houthi] advances in Dhalea could expose the southern hinterland, while [government advances] could threaten Houthi positions and supply routes towards Ibb, al-Bayda and, farther north, Sanaa,” al-Jeddawy noted.

With the escalating fighting, the Houthis face pressure on several fronts, but the group has been readying for a range of scenarios, Khaled Ghorab, a pro-Houthi general, said.

“The [Houthi] Yemeni armed forces were never caught off guard by the prospect of escalation; rather, they worked to build and develop their own military capabilities based on tactical combat plans designed to counter a comprehensive, sustained attack launched simultaneously from land, sea and air,” he said.

Ghorab noted that this state of readiness enables the Houthi forces to carry out a direct response to sources of the threat – whether deep within enemy territory or at sea – targeting military bases or aircraft carriers as far as the Horn of Africa.

While the warring parties compete to seize strategic positions on several front lines, the latest escalation is also closely related to the wider regional confrontation.

“Iran has an interest in keeping Yemen and the Red Sea active as sources of leverage, while parts of the government camp believe the Houthis are under growing strain and that this is an opportunity to weaken them,” al-Jeddawy, the Sanaa-based researcher, said.

“The escalation still reflects domestic military and political aims, but its timing and direction cannot be separated from the regional war,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Cattle were left behind in Hong Kong centuries ago; a 2026 genome study found their DNA holds a record of how livestock adapted to island life
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Hong Kong’s feral cattle are more than animals that escaped human care. Their genomes preserve a detailed record of how cattle can change after becomi.
articles.body: Hong Kong’s feral cattle are more than animals that escaped human care. Their genomes preserve a detailed record of how cattle can change after becoming separated from managed herds and exposed to natural pressures. A study titled ‘The genome landscape of Hong Kong feral cattle as a unique genetic resource,’ examined the animals using high-coverage whole-genome sequencing, allowing researchers to investigate their origins, genetic diversity and adaptation in greater detail than earlier studies. The findings reveal a population shaped by ancient cattle movements, wild-cattle ancestry, geographical isolation and the demands of living without the protection normally provided by farmers.Hong Kong feral cattle’s DNA revealed a distinct genetic historyThe analysis found that Hong Kong feral cattle form a genetically distinct population. They were most closely associated with East Asian indicine cattle, while also showing genetic patterns that set them apart from the other groups examined.The researchers found evidence that limited contact with mainland cattle meant that genes were not regularly introduced from outside populations. This helped create a more uniform genetic pattern within the Hong Kong cattle and separated them from their domestic ancestors.The study also found signs of inbreeding. The cattle had more long stretches of matching DNA than other indicine populations examined, indicating that animals with relatively close genetic relationships had reproduced over generations. Their effective population size(an estimate of how many animals are contributing genetically to future generations) has also been small.What was the methodology used by scientists to approach the research There are about 1,000 feral cattle in Hong Kong today, according to the study. Their recent history began when cattle farming declined during rapid urbanisation and economic development in the 1970s. The animals were left to roam freely and gradually became a feral population, meaning they were no longer managed in the way domestic cattle normally are.That change created unusual conditions. Instead of being selected mainly by farmers for production or other preferred traits, the cattle had to cope with disease, environmental pressures and finding mates without human control. The researchers noted that the animals also show striking variation in features such as horn shape, coat colour, hump size, tail length and body form.The research team sequenced the complete genomes of 30 Hong Kong feral cattle. They then compared the results with 116 cattle representing European taurine, Northeast Asian taurine, East Asian indicine and South Asian indicine populations.Ancient wild cattle left their mark on the feral onesThe story goes back much further than the period when the animals became feral. The researchers found evidence that the ancestry of Hong Kong cattle includes contributions from banteng and gaur, two wild bovine species.The study estimated that banteng ancestry accounts for roughly 10.74% to 11.81% of the Hong Kong cattle genome, while gaur ancestry contributes about 9.70% to 11.08%. The researchers estimated that banteng introgression occurred around 8,900 years ago and gaur introgression around 9,900 years ago, although both estimates have wide uncertainty ranges.Importantly, these genetic exchanges happened before Hong Kong feral cattle diverged from other East Asian indicine populations. In other words, the wild-cattle contribution was already part of their deeper ancestry rather than something that happened after the cattle became feral in Hong Kong.The researchers found that genes inherited through this ancient mixing were associated with biological processes including oxygen transport and bitter taste receptor activity. This suggests that wild cattle may have contributed useful genetic material as domestic cattle spread into new environments across Asia.Heat and survival shaped the modern population of feral cattle in Hong KongThe most revealing part of the study concerns changes that appear to have occurred under more recent environmental pressures. Researchers identified genetic regions showing signs of positive selection in the Hong Kong cattle, particularly those associated with heat tolerance, bone strength and coat colour.One notable signal involved the ADRA1A gene. The researchers linked this region to recovery from heat stress. The finding is particularly relevant because the cattle live without the heat-management measures available to farmed animals.Another important signal involved B4GALNT3, a gene associated with bone health and survival in wild conditions. The Hong Kong cattle carried a distinct pattern at this gene compared with the other cattle populations studied, suggesting that natural pressures may have favoured particular variants.The study therefore provides a picture of adaptation taking place without deliberate breeding. Traits that helped animals cope with heat, physical demands and other pressures could become more common as individuals carrying useful genetic variants survived and reproduced.Coat colour also carries clues of genetic lineageThe cattle’s varied coats offered another opportunity to investigate their genetic differences. The researchers identified copy-number changes (sections of DNA that occur in different numbers between individuals) associated with black and yellow coat colours.Three genes, NINL, DEXI and CIITA, were among those linked to differentiated regions. Black cattle had higher copy numbers in the relevant regions than yellow cattle, leading the researchers to suggest that these genes may contribute to the coat-colour differences seen in the population.However, the study does not present these findings as final proof. The researchers stressed that the functional effects of the candidate regions still need to be tested directly.Conservation value of this small feral population in Hong Kong The findings also raise concerns about the future of Hong Kong’s feral cattle. Their small effective population size and increased inbreeding could make the population more vulnerable over time, even though the animals still possess considerable genetic diversity.The study also has limitations. The researchers noted that they lacked cattle-specific data on open chromatin, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how some non-coding genetic variants affect gene activity. Several candidate regions, including those linked to coat colour, will require further lab and animal studies.Even so, the genome analysis offers an unusual record of what happens when livestock are released from long-term human management. Hong Kong’s cattle did not simply remain unchanged after becoming feral. Their genetic history records ancient wild-cattle contributions, prolonged isolation and selection for traits that may help them survive independently.For the researchers, that makes the population a valuable genetic resource. Its DNA shows how cattle can retain diversity while becoming genetically distinct, and how natural pressures can gradually shape animals that once depended heavily on people.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A 1950s farm pond at one of Georgia's busiest parks had leaking banks, failing pipes and decades of sediment; Roswell spent $3.1 million rebuilding it to manage runoff from 52 acres
articles.summary: US News: A farm pond built in the 1950s at Roswell Area Park in Georgia has reopened after a nearly year-long restoration. The $3.1 million project rebuilt the.
articles.body: A farm pond built in the 1950s at Roswell Area Park in Georgia has reopened after a nearly year-long restoration. The $3.1 million project rebuilt the pond’s embankment, replaced ageing stormwater infrastructure, removed decades of sediment and restored the walking trail around the water.According to North Atlanta Star, the pond is part of one of Roswell’s busiest public parks and receives runoff from a 52-acre drainage area. Over the years, problems developed beneath the surface. Tree roots weakened the earthen embankment, allowing water to escape, while old corrugated metal pipes and damaged retaining walls added to the problems.The restoration was designed to address those issues while improving the pond’s ability to handle stormwater. Crews also added new landscaping, 35 trees and habitat features for turtles. The work began in fall 2025 and continued through the winter and summer before the pond reopened on Thursday.The pond had originally been built as a farm pond, long before the surrounding land became a public park. As the area developed, the pond became part of Roswell Area Park, which now covers about 93 acres and includes athletic fields, tennis courts, a pool, playgrounds, a recreation centre and visual arts facilities.Why the pond needed restorationThe pond’s earthen embankment had been weakened by tree roots, creating places where water could leak out. The corrugated metal pipes had also deteriorated, while retaining walls had suffered damage.At the same time, sediment had accumulated on the pond floor over decades. This reduced the depth of the water and limited the amount of stormwater the pond could store.That was important because the pond receives runoff from a 52-acre drainage area. It was not originally designed as a modern stormwater facility, meaning its ageing structures had limited ability to control water during heavy rainfall.The city rebuilt the embankment and upgraded the stormwater system with reinforced concrete pipes, reconstructed outlet structures and additional storage capacity.Dredging removed decades of sedimentOne of the major parts of the restoration was dredging. Crews removed material that had built up on the bottom of the pond over many years.Removing the sediment increased the pond’s depth and storage capacity. It also cleared pollutants and debris that could affect water quality.The southern embankment near the Bill Johnson Community Activity Building was also reconstructed. Trees whose roots had contributed to leakage were removed, after which the area was rebuilt, graded and planted.The new landscape includes 35 trees, native shrubs and groundcover. These plants were selected to help stabilise the soil and support wildlife around the pond.The city also added logs and other habitat structures near the water for turtles. Turtles have already begun returning to the restored pond, along with frogs.Walking trail and habitat restoredThe walking trail around the pond was also restored, bringing back a route that many park visitors use while walking through the area.The pond is located close to several of the park’s other facilities rather than in a separate natural area. Its closure meant visitors could continue using most of Roswell Area Park but could not access one of its quieter walking and wildlife-viewing areas.With the work complete, visitors can again walk around the pond and watch the wildlife. The new plantings and habitat structures are intended to support the area as it recovers.Fishing will return laterBefore the pond was drained, fish were moved as part of the restoration work. The city plans to gradually restock the pond with native fish species, but fishing will not resume immediately after the reopening.The water and habitat need time to stabilise before the fish population can be rebuilt in phases. Fishing is currently expected to return in late summer or autumn 2027.That means the reopening marks the return of public access, but the ecological restoration is not yet complete. People can once again use the trail and observe wildlife while the pond’s aquatic habitat continues to recover.The project was funded through Roswell’s voter-approved 2022 bond programme, which is supporting improvements to parks and public facilities across the city.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Philippine ferry fire: Survivor recalls being trampled as he made narrow escape
articles.summary: A survivor has told the BBC of the chaos onboard as the ferry caught fire near the popular tourist spot of Coron.
articles.body:
Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.

Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.

Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.

Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.

Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell.

"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.

He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.

He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.

"When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.

Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water.

"It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.

Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.

According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday.

But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.

The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.

The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.

Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.

The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.

As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.

Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.

Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.

Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says.

"I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."

Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.

A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".

Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.

Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital.

"He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.

She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.

Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.

But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire.

On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there.

But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for.

"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone.

"I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."

articles.title: Benjamin Netanyahu has overseen a genocide: In his telling, he’s a victim
articles.summary: Ahead of Israel’s national elections, Netanyahu reaches for an old playbook: grievance, blame-shifting and victimhood.
articles.body:
Benjamin Netanyahu is Israel’s most electorally successful — and longest-serving — prime minister. He has overseen Israel’s greatest internal security failure and a genocide in Gaza, yet clung on to power.

Now, as he heads to his 13th parliamentary election, Netanyahu is relying on an old strategy that he has deployed for years, critics say — responding to accusations that might normally end a political career with deflections, subterfuge and claims of victimhood.

In the last few days, a story carried by the Israeli daily Haaretz, claiming that the United Arab Emirates had given Netanyahu advance warning of the Hamas-led attack of 2023, has been met not with reflection, but with legal action, counter-accusations and claims of “foreign interference” in Israel’s elections.

A week earlier, Netanyahu oversaw the launch of a political advertisement likening himself to a bullied child.

In the video, a child is portrayed who – it is revealed – is being picked on by anti-Netanyahu classmates, with signs of “anyone but Bibi”, referring to Israel’s prime minister and leader of the right-wing Likud party.

Netanyahu has been prime minister for 18 years across three separate periods and has been widely acknowledged as a key player in shifting Israeli politics to the right.

But despite this, he has still been eager to use populist discourses to portray himself as fighting the establishment as a perpetual victim of the system.

Israeli political psychologist Neta Oren from George Mason University told Al Jazeera that self-victimisation is an important part of Netanyahu’s playbook, and this is continuing into his next election campaign.

“For years, he has presented himself as the representative of ‘the people’ against the elite. Populism works especially well from the opposition, but what happens when you are the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history?” she said.

“Netanyahu’s solution has been to blame his failures on other forces — particularly the ‘deep state’ — and to portray himself as their victim, just as he portrays his supporters as victims of the old elite.

“This can make him appear weak or ineffective as a leader, but the sense of victimhood among his base, and their animosity toward the old elite, is so strong that this framing can still be an effective political tool for maintaining their support.”

Recently, Netanyahu has appeared to compete with the country’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for the legacy of the far-right Zionist militia Irgun, which was contained once the first Israeli government, led by David Ben-Gurion, came to power in 1949.

Rival news conferences have been held by the two Israeli party leaders to commemorate the “oppression” of the militia, which was responsible for the deaths of hundreds of Palestinian civilians and British soldiers during the Palestinian Mandate period.

These tactics appear drawn from the same political playbook as those used by populist politicians across the world: to ally themselves with those who feel opposed to the state and distance themselves from their previous scandals.

Earlier this month, Netanyahu attempted to deflect blame for his alleged failures ahead of and during the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, claiming that “defence officials” had deliberately chosen not to wake him during the first hours of an attack that he would otherwise have contained.

His wife Sara Netanyahu appeared to go further, suggesting to the pro-government Channel 14 last month that opposition leader and former General Yair Golan’s reaction to the assault — when he woke up and drove directly to the site of the attack — suggested that he must have known of Hamas’s plans in advance.

Such methods have been used by other politicians, such as United States President Donald Trump, Hungary’s Viktor Orban and India’s Narendra Modi. But Netanyahu’s use of victimisation by the “establishment” goes back further to around when former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995, claiming that Israel’s left had forgotten what it meant to be Jewish.

Analysts describe Netanyahu’s particular brand of populism as intended for a specifically Israeli audience and a shared sense of Zionist and Jewish identity among his party’s Likud base.

Similarly, many of Likud’s supporters are Mizrahi, drawn from migrants from across the Middle East and North Africa and typically come from lower-income backgrounds. They are attuned through experience as seeing themselves opposed to the Ashkenazi European establishment in Israel, something Netanyahu has been eager to feed on.

Dani Filc, a professor at Ben Gurion University and author of the book Hegemony and Populism in Israel, said that Netanyahu’s claim to victimhood is a common feature in populist narratives.

“Populism builds on a victimised people … His acting out of victimhood echoes with the fact that many Likud supporters have a collective memory of being excluded and sometimes oppressed by the mainly Ashkenazi establishment, and also plays with Jewish collective memory as victims,” he told Al Jazeera.

This discourse has dominated Netanyahu’s repeated confrontations with the judiciary and media since 2023.

Both Netanyahu’s 2020 corruption trial and his judicial overhaul have been cast by the Israeli right-wing not as legal or constitutional processes, but as a battle against a so-called unelected “deep state”, with its members, they claim, including the media and judiciary.

Daniel Bar-Tal, professor of psychology at Tel Aviv University, said this narrative has allowed him to distance himself from government failures.

“Netanyahu desires the status of victim,” Bar-Tal told Al Jazeera.

“He blames the deep state that he built, the officers that he nominated … just to be clean and not responsible. To be a victim has many advantages. You can be a perpetrator, you can disengage from ethical norms, and so on.”

articles.title: Charlie Kirk's 10 most powerful moments from college campuses to the Republican National Convention
articles.summary: From his Politicon debate with Hasan Piker to Bill Maher's "Club Random" podcast, the 10 most memorable Charlie Kirk moments before his assassination.
articles.body: Thursday marked the one-year anniversary of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk's assassination during a campus event at Utah Valley University in 2025. From college debates to national addresses, here are some of the most memorable moments of Kirk engaging in a free exchange of ideas during his life as a political activist: 1. Politicon debate with Hasan Piker During a 2018 Politicon debate with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who previously worked for "The Young Turks," Kirk called out Piker for pushing socialist policies without being willing to "give 95% of your money away and go live on a commune" in solidarity. "I live what I practice. I am a free-market capitalist," Kirk said. "I employ people. I took a risk. I have my own startup business. Every single day I practice what I preach. He wants other people to contribute to what he considers to be a good idea, what he considers will make the world a better place. You have the freedom to go live as a socialist. Go do it, Hasan. What's stopping you?" ‘KIRKIVERSARY’ CHARLIE KIRK LOOK-ALIKE CONTEST ADVERTISED AT UNIVERSITY OF SOUTH CAROLINA TO MARK KILLING 2. Charlie Kirk explains why he goes to college campuses During one of his many college campus debates in 2024, Kirk was approached by a student asking if he felt "silly" debating college students while being a man in his 30s. "So I vote and you vote. So I'm talking to voters of this country that will determine the future of Western civilization. That's what I'm doing here, too," Kirk said. 3. ‘Open mic’ for opponents At another debate that same year, Kirk was confronted by a student who accused him of being a "fascist." Kirk challenged the student to name one belief he held that qualified as "fascist." The student was unable to immediately think of one. "I'm such a bad fascist I let the people who disagree with me an open mic to talk to me for two hours uninterrupted. I'm an awful fascist," Kirk joked. 4. ‘This is feminism’ Kirk surprised the hosts of "The Iced Coffee Hour" in 2025 after he said, "Under no circumstance ever should a man ever let a woman pay for a date," even if he intends to marry her. When they asked if it would be considered a "nice gesture" for a woman to pay for a date, Kirk disagreed, emphasizing that a woman is meant to be provided for by a man. "This is feminism. Feminism is that you have to be this like self-independent," Kirk said. "It's not a nice gesture. It's you trying to be like egalitarian. No. You, as a woman, should want to be provided for. In fact, you should have an expectation that you, as a woman, are so important and so critical and so necessary and beautiful that it shouldn't even be a question." INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES 5. ‘Club Random’ with Bill Maher Just months before his assassination, Kirk appeared on Bill Maher's "Club Random" podcast where the two discussed deep topics, including the existence of God. Maher, a well-known atheist, remarked that "nobody knows" whether there is a God. "Do you hope you're wrong? That's the most important question," Kirk asked. "That's a great question," Maher replied. "Do you hope there's a heaven?" Kirk followed. "I hope they figure out how I can live forever. I like it here with you, Charlie, drinking this and smoking pot," Maher said. 6. Jubilee's ‘Surrounded’ debate Kirk took part in Jubilee's "Surrounded" series in 2024, which featured him pitted against 25 liberal college students. Early in the debate, Kirk was questioned about what should happen if a woman has a serious health complication during her pregnancy. Kirk countered by saying that the woman could have a C-section instead, flustering the female college student he was debating, who admitted she was not familiar with the procedure. "Cesarean section … it's a C-section. They do an insertion … they go right below the belly button, and they deliver the baby and that way she doesn't have to give birth. It's technically birth, but it's much safer. So that's actually safer than an abortion procedure." 7. Oxford University One of Kirk's last high-profile debates before his death was an appearance at Oxford University in August 2025. Before his comments, Kirk used his time to criticize an Oxford student for making what he said were inaccurate statements about President Donald Trump, including suggesting that he was deporting U.S. citizens. "I'll give you 1,000 pounds right now. If you could tell me the U.S. citizen that was deported under Donald Trump. You said that twice. The U.S. citizen that was deported under Donald Trump. Can anyone tell me, 1,000 pounds? I'll give it to you right now," Kirk said. He added, "That was a lie. You should know better than that. You go to Oxford." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE 8. Denouncing DEI At a 2025 Turning Point USA event, Kirk addressed his issues with diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies and explained his view of the conservative position to the crowd. "What we believe as conservatives is that skin color really doesn't matter that much. We care about character and merit. We want a country built on what you bring to the table, not how you look," Kirk said. "If you do something racist on top of something racist, that doesn't make the second racist action good," he added. 9. Abortion debate During another 2025 event, Kirk got into a heated debate with a student over the scale of abortion, which Kirk compared to the Holocaust. "It's 45 million babies. It's nearly eight times worse than the Holocaust. What's the moral difference between a small baby in the womb and a grown Jew who was killed at Auschwitz? What's the moral difference? One is older?" Kirk said. "One of them is a person," the student responded. "What species is the baby in the womb?" Kirk asked. "It's a human," the student answered. "Therefore, they should have human rights," Kirk said. 10. 2024 Republican National Convention Kirk spoke at the 2024 Republican National Convention in support of Trump's bid to return to the White House. During his remarks, he specifically highlighted the Gen Z audience watching him and informed them that national decline is a choice. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "You don't have to stay poor. You don't have to accept being worse off than your parents," Kirk said. "You don't have to feel aimless and unhappy. You don't have to support leaders who lied to you and took advantage of you for your vote. America's future is a series of choices. Our current state of slow-motion national decline is a choice. This November, we're going to choose success."

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer reveals post-mistrial strategy as retrial looms
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington reveals his strategy after the mistrial, urging prosecutors to pursue treatment instead of prison while appealing to President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Kevin Reddington is laying out an aggressive, multipronged strategy to keep Lindsay Clancy from facing another jury — and, ultimately, from going to prison — as prosecutors weigh whether to retry the Massachusetts mother after last month's mistrial. In his first interview with Fox News since the jury deadlocked after seven weeks of testimony, Clancy's attorney detailed his plans to challenge any retrial in court, push prosecutors to reduce the charges, seek a bench trial instead of a jury trial and argue for psychiatric treatment rather than incarceration. A Norfolk Superior Court jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict last month, prompting Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial. Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to charges stemming from the 2023 deaths of her three children. Prosecutors have not yet announced whether they will retry the case. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR WHO BACKED THE DEFENSE ALSO PUBLICLY CHEERED KAREN READ'S ACQUITTAL Reddington said his first priority is arguing later this month that a retrial would violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy because the mistrial was declared over the defense's objection. If that effort fails, he said he hopes Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz will reduce the charges to second-degree murder, so Clancy could waive her right to a jury trial and instead have her case decided by a judge. "I would like to see Tim reduce it to a second degree... and fashion something where Lindsay gets the mental, physical help that she needs rather than criminal prosecution, because I would not ever, ever in a million years have that woman go to Framingham State Prison," Reddington said. He said he would seek a sentence centered on probation and mandatory psychiatric treatment in a secure facility rather than incarceration. LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT Reddington also stood by his criticism of the lone holdout juror, rejecting accusations that his post-trial remarks amounted to intimidation. "I was angry because of his refusal to follow the law," Reddington told Fox News. "That's what I was angry about. That's why I felt that the other jurors, after their seven-week sacrifice, were robbed. That's why I felt for Lindsay, because she deserved to have the verdict that she was entitled to." He added that he would have defended the juror's right to hold firm if he had simply disagreed with the other 11 jurors on the merits of the case. "If this guy just said, 'look, I think the government proved their case, and I'm not bending,' I would be the first person to defend his right to do that because that's the jury system," Reddington insisted. Reddington also renewed his call for President Donald Trump to weigh in, saying he hopes the president will personally urge Cruz not to pursue another trial. "I'd like the president to pick up the phone and speak with Tim Cruz," Reddington said. "If you do that, that'd be great. I mean, they're both Republicans." Reddington argued such a conversation would not be improper because the decision over whether to retry Clancy rests with the district attorney, calling it "an executive decision." Despite repeatedly criticizing Cruz in the days following the mistrial, Reddington also offered a pair of rare public concessions, saying he regretted accusing the district attorney of not knowing the names of Clancy's three children and boasting that he had "crushed" him at trial. "I had no right to accuse the man of not knowing the names of those kids and I regret that," Reddington said. Reddington also said he "probably should have used a different set of words" after declaring he had "crushed" Cruz, adding that he should have simply said he believed the defense presented the stronger case while emphasizing that the burden of proof rested with the prosecution. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The comments mark one of Reddington's first public acknowledgments that he went too far in some of his post-trial remarks, even as he continues to press for a resolution that prioritizes treatment over incarceration.

articles.title: From voter ID to $5,000 cheques: Trump goes desi, mimics India’s election toolkit
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump may never admit it, but it’s self-evident. The self-proclaimed oldest democracy is beginning to borrow from political toolki.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump may never admit it, but it’s self-evident. The self-proclaimed oldest democracy is beginning to borrow from political toolkits of the world’s largest democracy.It first reflected in Trump’s obsession with photo identification for voting. Now comes the promise of money.$5,000 Trump dividendIt’s scene which is quite familiar for Indians. Come election time and it starts raining freebies for voters. The template works like this: Make promises first and then do economic calculations later, once you have won the polls.Now, something similar is happening in US.At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump offered voters a strikingly transactional proposition: Return Republicans to power in Congress and every adult American citizen could receive $5,000.“Pretend that I’m on the ballot just one more time,” Trump told supporters.“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate...I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said.“It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. “Now all we have to do is win.”With potentially more than 200 million payments, Trump could be promising well over $1 trillion in “dividends” unless the programme is restricted by income or other eligibility criteria, a WSJ report said.There is little chance that a $1 trillion-plus payout would sail through Congress at a moment when US public debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time and is already pushing up borrowing costs.But as political messaging, the promise matters. For anyone familiar with Indian elections, the formula feels instantly recognisable.Make voter identity a major political issue. Build databases capable of identifying citizens and beneficiaries. Deliver welfare directly rather than through opaque bureaucracies. Brand the benefit aggressively. And, most importantly, make sure the voter knows exactly which government put the money in the account.Trump, in other words, appears to be discovering the politics of Indian-style direct welfare.From welfare to political technologyIndia’s welfare state has changed dramatically over the past decade. The Modi government’s Direct Benefit Transfer(DBT) changed that relationship.Money began arriving straight into bank accounts. A voter receiving Rs 2,000 directly into a bank account does not need a politician to explain government policy. That is electoral gold.Indian states took the idea further.Cash assistance for girls and women has become one of the most powerful electoral instruments in recent times.Madhya Pradesh’s Ladli Behna programme, Maharashtra’s Ladki Bahin scheme and similar initiatives elsewhere turned women not merely into welfare recipients but into a distinct political constituency.Indian politicians have understood that modern welfare is not merely about how much governments spend. It is about how clearly citizens can identify the sender.That is the political insight hiding inside Trump’s $5,000 proposal.However, Tump's dividend is not identical to India's DBT schemes: It targets no specific demographic and depends on a Congress that shows no appetite for it. But the underlying instinct is the same one Indian incumbents have refined: Convert a government or leader's flagging popularity into a direct, personal payment timed to the ballot box, and let voters decide whether to reward the giver.ID first, benefits laterThe other Indian parallel is Trump’s push for tougher voter identification. In his March 2025 executive order overhauling federal election procedures, Trump explicitly cited India and Brazil for linking voter identity to biometric databases, contrasting them with an American system that leans on self-attestation of citizenship.In August, Trump again posted on Truth Social about photo ID cards."We need to pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT, now!" Trump wrote, invoking legislation that would mandate citizenship proof and government-issued photo ID for federal voting.His administration has repeatedly argued that US elections require stronger proof of identity and citizenship.However, India’s system is more complicated than that comparison suggests.The Electors Photo Identity Card, or EPIC, is widely used, but it is not the sole document voters can present. The Election Commission accepts several alternative photo identification documents, and Aadhaar is not mandatory for voting.The US also does not start from zero. Most states already have some form of voter identification requirement.Still, politically, Trump is assembling two ideas that sit comfortably together in the Indian political imagination: Prove who the voter is and then deliver benefits directly to that person.A president under pressureTrump has promised to campaign aggressively for Republicans and he is expected to make about 35 trips on behalf of candidates in closely fought races. He is also directing his political action committee to deploy some of the hundreds of millions of dollars it has raised in key contests, a Bloomberg report said.There is no doubt that Trump is feeling the heat. Polling shows Americans unconvinced by Trump's insistence that affordability complaints are overblown, and Wednesday's convention drew visible empty seats as vulnerable Republican candidates skipped the event altogether.Trump’s popularity is at all-time low and he has entangled US in what seems to be a forever war with Iran.But politically, the message is unmistakable. Faced with the prospect of losing Congress and spending the remainder of his presidency as a lame duck, Trump appears increasingly willing to borrow from India’s electoral playbook.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2013, Paris tested spraying non-drinking water on sun-baked streets; wet pavement was up to 23°F cooler, but the effect faded as the surface dried
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Paris's innovative pavement watering program significantly reduces street temperatures and offers a temporary cooling solution during heatwaves, alongside historical context and modern implications for urban environments.
articles.body: Long before anyone worried about climate change, Parisian street cleaners doused the city's pavements with water every morning, a practice dating back to the late nineteenth century that was originally meant to keep dust down rather than cool anyone off. That habit faded through the twentieth century as cleaning methods changed, and the practice became a historical curiosity. The deadly heatwave that swept across Europe in August 2003, causing tens of thousands of excess deaths across the continent and hitting the Paris region particularly hard, led city planners to rethink almost every tool in their toolbox to keep residents safe during extreme heat, including tools that had quietly fallen out of favour.This rethinking led the City of Paris to test whether spraying non-drinking water onto sunny streets could significantly ease heat stress for people walking in the city during a heatwave, and in the summer of 2013, it launched an experimental pavement watering programme. Their main testing ground was a stretch of Rue du Louvre, a wide, lightly shaded street near Les Halles that is exposed to direct sun for much of the day, but they later expanded their experiments to the Belleville district as well.Cooling of a hot street in real time The process of pavement watering is simple: evaporative cooling, the same principle that makes a person feel cold when stepping out of a swimming pool on a breezy day. When water evaporates, it takes up a massive amount of energy, and if that water is sitting on a sun-baked road surface, the evaporation process pulls heat out of the pavement itself rather than letting it build up and radiate back into the air around it. According to research on the official Ville de Paris website, doctoral research conducted between 2013 and 2015 found that watering could reduce exposed surface temperatures by around fifteen degrees Celsius during sunny periods, while also noticeably lowering how hot pedestrians felt as they walked through treated areas.Field measurements recorded surface-temperature reductions of up to 13 degrees Celsius, or roughly 23 degrees Fahrenheit, during direct sunlight, compared with reductions of up to 4 degrees Celsius when the pavement was shaded. Researchers used infrared cameras to track these changes in close to real time, which let them spot the exact moment a wet patch of road began drying out, since the surface temperature would spike sharply the instant standing water disappeared.Cooling effect that quickly fades away as water evaporatesThis increase in drying was one of the most important findings of the Paris trials. Watering pavement has a powerful but short-lived cooling effect, and researchers found that uninterrupted watering was necessary during periods of direct sunlight to keep the benefit. A study published in the Journal of Sustainable Development of Energy, Water and Environment Systems confirmed this pattern, noting that pavement watering lowered surface temperatures for several hours after each application and reduced how quickly heat was released from the pavement near sunset, but that the cooling effect could not simply be applied once and left to last through the entire afternoon.This pragmatic constraint shaped the way the city refined the programme in summers thereafter. Rather than watering continuously regardless of conditions, engineers sought to optimise the timing and amount of water used. The method relies on a separate non-drinking water network fed from the Seine and the Canal de l'Ourcq, a resource that Paris has maintained since the nineteenth century for uses such as street cleaning and irrigation that do not require treated drinking water.Lessons for other cities looking for a low-tech cooling fixPavement watering will never replace shade, green cover or structural redesign as a long-term strategy for cooling cities, and Paris researchers have been frank that the effect is temporary and resource intensive to maintain across a large area. But its beauty is that it can be deployed rapidly in an acute emergency, using infrastructure that many cities already have, whether that is a dedicated non-potable network such as the one in Paris or even ordinary municipal water trucks. The Paris experience is a useful reminder for cities across South Asia, which are seeing more frequent and severe heatwaves and which often have their own separate non-drinking water systems for irrigation and cleaning, that sometimes the quickest relief available during a dangerous heat spell is also one of the oldest tricks in a city’s toolkit, even if it has to be repeated again and again to keep working.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday invited France and other nations to be a \"co-traveller\" in the next phase of the country's space r.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday invited France and other nations to be a "co-traveller" in the next phase of the country's space research. He was virtually addressing the International Space Summit in Paris."We invite France and other nations to be our co-traveller in next phase of space research," he said, adding that "France has been trusted partner in India's space programme since 1960s".Speaking about Isro's success, he said, "Chandrayaan-3 made India the first nation to land near the lunar South Pole. Aditya L-1 is unlocking the secrets of the Sun. Last year, an Indian visited the International Space Station. Looking ahead, we aim to establish an Indian space station by 2035 and send an Indian to the moon by 2040. In all these efforts, our guiding principles have been clear. Their benefits must reach all humanity.""Alongside ISRO, India's private space sector is also surging in a big way. The energy of enterprise is joining the excellence of ISRO. France has been a trusted partner since the Indian space program began in the 1960s. Today, our cooperation spans Earth observation and advanced technologies, uniting scientific excellence with human purpose. We invite France and the world to be co-travellers in India's next space frontier. Let the Space Summit in Paris send a clear message that we will explore together, innovate together and protect space together for all humanity and for generations to come. I convey my best wishes to all the participants," he added.Describing India's space philosophy, he said, "India's approach is rooted in 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'. That is one Earth, one family, one future. This spirit must now travel beyond Earth. We support a safe, secure, peaceful, and sustainable space domain anchored in international law, dialogue, and multilateral cooperation. Scientific data must serve the common good with openness and integrity. India's space journey reflects this philosophy."The first International Space Summit in Paris has brought together governments, space agencies, companies and scientists to strengthen international cooperation and make space activities a long-term driver of societal development. articles.title: Russia’s new shelling tactics deepen suffering in Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainians are losing more sleep, shopping for food is becoming harder and travel is often fraught with risk and delays.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – When Olena Krakovska is at work selling tools for manicures from a small shop on the basement floor of a shopping centre in central Kyiv, she doesn’t hear or see much.

“I’m already in a bomb shelter. Air raid or not, I’m at work,” the 42-year-old single mother of two boys told Al Jazeera.

Outside there are regular wailing air raid sirens, red-and-white explosions of Russian drones hit by Ukrainian interceptors, gong-like thuds and white plumes of smoke swelling in the sky.

Falling debris, from tiny metal pieces to larger fragments of fuselage, flop in the wind and come down with the sour stench of gunpowder.

But when Krakovska is at home, the air raids rattle her senses and nerves.

“There’s been too many recently. My brain isn’t functioning, my movements are uncoordinated,” she said.

Since mid-August, Russian air raids in Ukraine have become longer, more frightening for residents and more frequent as part of Moscow’s new tactic aimed at “terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 6.

Between June and early August, there were five air raids a week with a combined duration of 2.3 hours, according to a calculation by the UA.news web portal. In the third week of August, their number rose to 12 and their duration to 7.9 hours, and in the fourth week, 34 over 23.2 hours.

Early September brought a brief lull – Russia stopped shelling Kyiv for three days when United States negotiators visited Moscow and Kyiv.

But on Monday, shelling resumed with a six-hour air raid, killing five, wounding 35 and causing several fires.

Each raid involves fewer drones and missiles, but the timing is unpredictable, keeping hundreds of thousands awake all night and paralysing all walks of daily life.

They interrupt office hours, business meetings and school lessons, traumatise people and cause long traffic jams. They also turn commutes on public transport into hours-long ordeals.

Stoicism, a macabre sense of humour and ingenuity keep Ukrainians optimistic.

“There’s no way out, only when you’re in a coffin,” Krakovska quipped.

That’s a phrase she heard from her great-grandmother Serafima, who survived the 1932-33 Holodomor famine and the 1941-43 Nazi occupation of central Ukraine.

“She saw things that were way worse than what we’re living through,” Krakovska said.

What worries her during her working hours is not the air raids but the schooling of her sons Bohdan, 12, and Volodymyr, 10.

Their academic year began on September 1, but after two days spent in the airless school basement-turned-bomb shelter, she decided that they should study online, at home, in front of laptops.

But video games are just a click away, and the boys can barely focus on what their teachers say.

“They don’t socialise with friends, don’t play outdoors. They bicker. They pay less attention to their classes and homework,” she sighed.

Krakovska lives on the left bank of the Dnipro river that bisects Kyiv and is up to a kilometre (0.62 miles) wide.

She used to spend 45 minutes getting to work by subway listening to music, scrolling through social media or reading e-books.

But Kyiv authorities stop the movement of subway trains across the Dnipro during air raids – and crowds of frustrated commuters spend hours in subway stations or nearby.

One day in late August, Krakovska, like hundreds of other exhausted people, spent almost three hours waiting for the train inside a station.

She kept checking the Telegram channels that report the progress of air raids, worried about her phone’s dying battery and her sons’ safety.

Her shopping habits have also changed. She no longer idles in supermarkets looking for discounts – Russian attacks have destroyed several warehouses, leading to some food and medicine shortages.

“You still can buy anything, but you need to spend more time looking,” she said.

These days, she quickly buys food from small vendors next to the shopping mall or her apartment building.

One of them is Olha Bondar, 49, who owns a tiny fruit and vegetable stand in an underground pass.

She has begun to earn a bit more – but the war consumes every extra kopeck she makes.

She and her son Vadym fled Volnovakha, an eastern town with a pre-war population of about 20,000, days before it was occupied by Russian forces in 2022.

Most of Volnovakha lies in ruins, including her grandfather’s house where she grew up playing with her siblings and cousins, weeding beds of beets and tomatoes and throwing Colorado potato beetles into a tin can with gasoline.

The black and orange beetles “look like St George’s ribbons,” one of Russia’s main ideological symbols now ubiquitous in occupied Ukrainian regions, she said with a grimace of disgust.

Some of her relatives have not left because of their pro-Moscow sympathies.

“They blame Kyiv and the West for all the death, destruction and squalor around them,” Bondar said with a shrug.

She does not mind the air raid sirens as long as she gets text messages from her 24-year-old son who volunteered to enlist in 2023 and serves in northern Ukraine.

“I hear his voice or read his texts – and nothing else matters,” she said, before weighing a kilogramme of velvet-blue plums.

She lives in a rented one-bedroom apartment. But more affluent Kyiv residents have fled for the suburbs, renting or buying houses with wood stoves, wells and cool, dark basements to store food.

“We just can’t find a house, they don’t let people with pets in, and we have two fox terriers,” Roman, a software engineer who withheld his last name because his main client is a defence company, told Al Jazeera.

He and his partner Alisa, a yoga instructor who switched to online lessons, feel stranded in their two-bedroom apartment on the eighth floor of a nine-storey building.

After recently enduring a 3.5-hour traffic jam, Roman prefers to talk to his colleagues and clients on Zoom.

He also said his mental health is affected; he has started taking antidepressants and sleeping pills.

“Otherwise I just lie awake listening and thinking, listening and thinking,” he said while his dogs rummaged in the grass near his apartment building.

“And his tossing and turning drives me nuts,” Alisa quipped.

But they keep adapting and thinking ahead because the coming winter will bring more strikes on energy infrastructure and exhausting blackouts.

“We got used to things we’d only seen in horror movies,” she said.

articles.title: Calling Democrats ‘communists’ won’t win Gen Z — Republicans need a better offer
articles.summary: The first Republican midterm convention at the American Airlines Center has already brought real energy, but a Gen-Z conservative argues solutions must replace outrage.
articles.body: I’m sitting in the American Airlines Center as the first-ever Republican midterm convention gets underway in Dallas, and the energy is real. The room is loud. The crowd is locked in. People came here because they know November is not a drill. That’s the good news. The less comfortable news is this: just calling Democrats communists is not a strategy. Yes, they are. The agenda is collectivist. The instincts are coercive. The destination is bigger government, weaker families and a generation trained to look to the state for everything. But their lies, empty promises and dangling "free" things in front of my generation are working. Emotions work. Subsidized housing talking points work. Student-debt theater works. Climate panic works. Identity sermons work. They do not need to be honest. They need to be first, loud, and simple. I'M GEN Z: IF THE GOP WANTS MY VOTE, STOP THE SPEECHES AND FIX THE HOUSING CRISIS If our answer is just "they’re communists," we lose the people who never took a political theory class and never will. They hear the word, shrug and go back to the pitch that sounds like relief. We cannot keep crying about it from the sidelines. We have to offer something better, something that a 20-year-old like me can actually picture: work that pays, housing that is not a fantasy, energy that is cheap, schools that teach instead of lecture, streets that are safe and a government that stops treating ambition like a moral defect. This convention is the first time I have heard some of that from our side in a concentrated way. Not just contrast. Not just diagnosis. Actual counteroffers — tax relief that hits paychecks, border enforcement that is measurable, energy abundance instead of rationing and candidates who talk about building things instead of merely condemning the other tribe. REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG That is the part that matters. Name-calling is catharsis. Solutions are politics. Democrats have spent years selling feelings and subsidies. If Republicans spend the next eight weeks only selling outrage, we will walk into November with high energy and a losing argument. REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE MIDTERMS IF THEY JUST STOP UNDERSELLING SUCCESS Dallas should be the start of something, not a two-night pep rally. I hope this is not the last time before the midterms that our side talks like people who intend to govern, not just people who intend to be right. The other side is not winning because they are smarter. They are winning parts of my generation because they showed up with a story. We finally started answering with one. Don’t stop. YOUNG CONSERVATIVES REVEAL WHAT’S TOP OF MIND AS GOP, DEMOCRATS BATTLE FOR 'HOPELESS' GEN Z VOTERS The last year and a half gave us more than talking points. The no-tax-on-tips-and-overtime policy is showing up in real returns. Seniors got the promised Social Security tax relief. The Working Families Tax Cuts put money back in paychecks. The border is no longer a slogan: catch-and-release ended, interior releases went to zero for months, and the wall and agents finally got funded. Trump Accounts give kids a start on savings instead of debt mythology. Energy leasing came back. That is a record. Stop whispering it to donors and start saying it to 20-year-olds. MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400 After Dallas, President Trump should take this same arena energy on the road. Tour campuses. Pack college arenas the way this hall is filled. Do not wait for young voters to find a clip. Take our message to them. Put two slides behind him. First: promises kept, with checkmarks. Tips. Overtime. Senior relief. Tax cuts that hit filings. A closed border. Accounts for kids. American energy. Make them look at the list instead of a Democrat’s poster about "free." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Then put up the second slide: what Gen Z is still owed in the last two years of this term. Housing you can actually buy, not another voucher speech. Power bills that stop eating the paycheck. Trades and apprenticeships with the same dignity as a four-year degree. Colleges that compete on price and speech instead of ideology. First jobs that hire for work, not politics. Cities that feel safe enough to stay in. Ownership, not a new subscription to the state. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That is how you beat the other side’s offer. They sell cancellation, panic and belonging. We should sell keys, hours, watts and a wage. Dallas cannot be a two-night pep rally with a better diagnosis. Take the checkmarks on tour. Take the unfinished list with them. My generation has already heard the word communist. What we have not heard enough is a deal. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM BRILYN HOLLYHAND

articles.title: Florida man faces execution for 1996 killing connected to ‘Hog Trail Murders’
articles.summary: A Florida man convicted in one of a series of suspected killings that became known as the “Hog Trail Murders” in the 1990s was scheduled Thursday to become the state’s 15th person executed this year.
articles.body: A Florida man convicted in one of a series of suspected killings that became known as the “Hog Trail Murders” in the 1990s was scheduled Thursday to become the state’s 15th person executed this year. Daniel Owen Conahan Jr., 72, was sentenced to die for the 1996 kidnapping and strangling of Richard Allen Montgomery, whose mutilated body was found in a wooded southwest Florida area where authorities found the remains of at least six people over a three-year span. Conahan, who has maintained his innocence, has previously been identified by authorities as a person of interest in the other deaths, but he was never charged. He has argued the evidence against him was circumstantial. Conahan was scheduled to die by lethal injection in the nation’s busiest death chamber. Florida has carried out more than half of the 24 total executions in the U.S. so far this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January. Multiple bodies found in popular hunting area Conahan was arrested in July 1996 after local and state law enforcement officials spent more than two years investigating a series of homicides in which mutilated and decomposing bodies were discovered in a wooded area of Charlotte County, north of Fort Myers. As the number of bodies increased, so did media coverage. The deaths eventually were dubbed the “Hog Trail Murders” because of the swampy, wooded locations where the bodies were found. The case has been featured many times over the past three decades on true-crime television shows, YouTube channels and podcasts. The first body was found by hunters in February 1994, followed by at least five more bodies over the next three years. Most of the remains were severely decomposed, but investigators believed Montgomery had been dead for less than a day when he was found. Investigators eventually determined that the killer was targeting homeless men. Investigators found similarities in cases Detectives started looking into Conahan in 1996 after a man in prison for stealing Conahan’s car claimed that Conahan had lured him to a remote area and offered to pay him to pose for nude photos. The man said he drove off in the car after seeing a knife. Later, detectives learned about a case with similarities in Fort Myers, in which a victim claimed a man who offered cash for nude photos had tied him to a tree and attempted to strangle him. Conahan was initially arrested and charged with attempted murder, and several months later was also charged in Montgomery’s death. Conahan waived his right to a jury trial and was convicted by a judge of murder and kidnapping in August 1999. Conahan was never charged with any other homicides, but a sheriff’s office report about the investigation concluded that all of the victims discovered within a 10-mile (16-kilometer) radius were likely killed by the same person. In 2007, a land survey crew discovered eight bodies in Fort Myers. The four victims identified by authorities were homeless, and officials said they all suffered similar injuries to the Charlotte County victims. Investigators at the time publicly identified Conahan, who was already on Florida’s death row, as a person of interest, but he was never charged. The Florida Supreme Court last week denied Conahan’s final appeals, including one requesting additional testing on DNA collected from the victim. The court ruled that proving Montgomery had DNA on his body from someone other than Conahan wouldn’t exonerate him. A final appeal remains pending before the U.S. Supreme Court. Florida leads the way in executions A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Florida led the way with 19 lethal injections, a state record since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

articles.title: 'Everywoman' statue unveiled on Trafalgar Square's Fourth Plinth
articles.summary: Tschabalala Self's Lady in Blue will sit atop the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square for the next two years.
articles.body:
A sculpture inspired by a desire to bring a contemporary "everywoman" to Trafalgar Square has been unveiled on London's Fourth Plinth.

Lady In Blue by New York artist Tschabalala Self, which pays homage to a young, metropolitan woman, is the 16th artwork to feature on the plinth since 1998.

The bronze and blue figure replaces Mil Veces un Instante (A Thousand Times in an Instant) by Teresa Margolles.

The statue has been patinated with a pigment refined from Lapis Lazuli, a semi-precious stone that has been used by artists for millennia.

Self said she had set out to put an ordinary contemporary Londoner on a site more usually associated with statues of monarchs and military commanders.

"My work Lady In Blue will bring to Trafalgar Square a woman that many can relate to," the artist said.

"She is not an idol to venerate or a historic figurehead to commemorate.

"She is a woman walking forward into our collective future with ambition and purpose. She is a Londoner, who represents the city's spirit."

Self was named as the winning artist in March 2024, alongside Andra Ursuta, whose work is due to go up on the plinth in 2028.

Both were selected by the Fourth Plinth Commissioning Group, an independent panel chaired by the writer and curator Ekow Eshun.

She said: "Lady In Blue transforms the everyday into the monumental.

"Tschabalala Self takes the familiar figure of a woman moving through the city and gives her an extraordinary presence at the heart of London."

Justine Simons, the deputy mayor for culture and the creative industries, described the work as a striking addition to a historic part of the city.

Born in New York in 1990, Self works across painting, printmaking and sculpture, often using sewn and printed materials to build up depictions of the human figure.

She held her first institutional exhibition in London and later showed her first major painting series in the city.

The Fourth Plinth was left empty for more than 150 years after money ran out for an equestrian statue of William IV.

The commissioning programme was started by the RSA in 1998 and the first work, Mark Wallinger's Ecce Homo, went up the following year. A new sculpture has been installed roughly every two years since.

articles.title: Hong Kong court rules Dow Jones tried to stop journalist taking union role
articles.summary: Dow Jones was acquitted of the charge of dismissal over Selina Cheng’s leadership role.
articles.body:
A Hong Kong court has convicted Dow Jones for trying to deter a journalist from taking a union role, but also acquitted the publisher on the charge of dismissal over the role, in a case that raised concerns about media freedom in the city.

Selina Cheng , who was fired by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) in July 2024, had accused the newspaper’s publisher Dow Jones of unlawfully terminating her employment over her role chairing the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) and of trying to prevent her from standing for a union position.

The court found the company guilty on Thursday of trying to prevent Cheng’s right to run for the union chairmanship.

However, the judge sided with Dow Jones’ argument that she was made redundant because of corporate restructuring, and not due to her role as HKJA chair.

The right to take part in a trade union is protected by Hong Kong’s labour laws. An employer found guilty on “prevent or deter” charges could be fined up to 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,755).

“If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters,” Cheng told reporters outside the court after the ruling.

The judge said the company’s requirement that Cheng seek prior permission to take a union role was an “unjustified deterrent” of her rights.

Dow Jones said it disagreed with the ruling and was evaluating next steps.

“The Wall Street Journal has a long and proud history as an employer in Hong Kong. Throughout that time, we have remained deeply respectful of its labour laws and supportive of our employees’ rights, while publishing excellent, impartial journalism about the region,” a spokesperson said.

Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.

Cheng launched a private prosecution last year for illegal termination, after filing a complaint with the Labour Department that did not result in a prosecution.

Founded in 1968, the HKJA is Hong Kong’s longest-established journalists’ organisation and one of the last remaining groups advocating for media rights in the city.

Although Hong Kong was once known for its independent news outlets, media freedom has come under strain and many outlets have disbanded since Beijing imposed a 2020 national security law following sometimes violent pro-democracy protests, according to international rankings and HKJA surveys.

articles.title: Former Tory campaign chief pleads guilty over election bet
articles.summary: Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when the 2024 election would be held.
articles.body:
The Conservatives' former director of campaigning and his wife have pleaded guilty to cheating at gambling by placing bets on the date of the 2024 general election.

Anthony Lee passed confidential information to his wife Laura Lee about when former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was planning to call the general election.

Laura Lee, who was a parliamentary candidate at the time, then placed bets on the date of the general election.

On Thursday at Southwark Crown Court, Anthony Lee pleaded guilty to two offences and Laura Lee pleaded guilty to one offence. They will be sentenced in October.

The trials of 10 other defendants will take place in September 2027 and January 2028.

Former MP Craig Williams, who was Sunak's closest parliamentary aide at the time, pleaded guilty in June and will be sentenced at a later date.

In Williams' case, the prosecution said he bet £250, £100, and £22.50 on the date of the 2024 election, telling the court he "used highly sensitive and confidential information".

When details of the scandal first emerged in June 2024, Williams admitted making a "huge error of judgment".

Sunak's decision to call the poll was a surprise to many, including many Conservative MPs, who were expecting an autumn date.
